summary: Republishes PKCS #12 version 1.1, a syntax for transferring personal identity information such as private keys and certificates. It moves change control from RSA Laboratories to the IETF.

plainLanguage.summary: PKCS #12 defines a format for moving personal identity information, including private keys and certificates, between platforms. It describes ways to encrypt the information and check that it has not been changed.

questions: what is inside a pkcs12 file
subtitle: A portable container for moving keys, certificates, and related identity data.

tldr.problem: Users need to transfer personal identity information, such as private keys and certificates, between platforms while protecting privacy and detecting tampering.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #12 places typed bags inside a PFX structure and supports public-key or password-based privacy and integrity modes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7292 republishes PKCS #12 version 1.1 and transfers change control to the IETF. It was updated by RFC 9579 and RFC 9879; the older password privacy derivation method is not recommended for new use.

today: RFC 7292 is an Informational document updated by RFC 9579 and RFC 9879. It transfers PKCS #12 change control to the IETF and says its Appendix B method is not recommended for new password privacy use.

sections.title: Purpose and Publication
sections.content:
PKCS #12 v1.1 describes a transfer format for personal identity information, including private keys, certificates, secrets, and extensions. Supporting platforms can use it to import and export one set of this information.

RFC 7292 republishes the PKCS #12 specification from RSA Laboratories and transfers change control to the IETF. The document includes minor changes, such as additional hash algorithms and a recommendation to use PKCS #5 v2.1 rather than the Appendix B method for password privacy mode.
sections.plainLanguage: PKCS #12 provides a common format for transferring identity information between platforms. This RFC republishes version 1.1 under IETF change control and notes several changes.

sections.title: Privacy and Integrity Choices
sections.content:
The format combines one privacy mode with one integrity mode. Public-key privacy encrypts information for a known destination platform; password privacy encrypts it with a key derived from a user name and password. Public-key integrity uses a digital signature, while password integrity uses a Message Authentication Code (MAC).

All combinations are permitted. The RFC says public-key modes are generally preferable from a security viewpoint, but may not be possible when the destination is unknown at export time. The integrity wrapper covers the complete AuthenticatedSafe, including any unencrypted parts.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption hides the transferred information, while integrity protection helps reveal changes. Each can use a public key or a password, depending on what the platforms can arrange.

sections.title: PFX and Its Bags
sections.content:
The top-level PFX structure contains a version, an authSafe value, and optional MacData. This version requires PFX version 3. The AuthenticatedSafe holds a sequence of ContentInfo values, which can contain plaintext, password-encrypted data, or data encrypted for a public key.

Each SafeContents is a sequence of SafeBag entries. Six bag types hold a private key, an encrypted private key, a certificate, a certificate revocation list, a miscellaneous secret, or nested SafeContents. Optional attributes can provide a friendly name or local key identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A PFX contains one protected collection, which can contain smaller collections of labeled items. Those items can hold keys, certificates, revocation lists, or other secrets.

sections.title: Creating and Importing a PFX
sections.content:
To create a PFX, an application prepares one or more SafeContents values and wraps each as plaintext, password-encrypted data, or public-key-enveloped data. It places these values in an AuthenticatedSafe and then applies integrity protection with a signature or an HMAC.

Import reverses these steps. Applications should ignore object identifiers they do not recognize and may alert users about them. If an imported item would replace a local item, the application should handle that carefully and may ask the user what to do.
sections.plainLanguage: To export, an application groups the items, applies the selected privacy mode, and adds integrity protection. To import, it opens the structure and should take care before replacing existing information.

sections.title: Password-Based Protection
sections.content:
Password-based protection permits offline password searches against the methods in this document. Salt and an iteration count can make attacks more costly, but the RFC stresses choosing and protecting passwords carefully.

The Appendix B key-derivation method is not recommended for new password privacy use; PKCS #5 v2.1 should be used instead. The older method remains in use for password integrity mode and for backward compatibility. The RFC recommends an iteration count of 1024 or more and a random salt ideally as long as the hash output.
sections.plainLanguage: Password protection can be attacked by trying guesses away from the system. Strong passwords, salt, and repeated work make that harder, and the RFC recommends a newer derivation method for password privacy.
